771.title: Nachiketa at Death's door
771.hook: a boy waits three days at Death's house and asks what happens after
771.howItsDone: Hindus study the Katha Upanishad as scripture, often with a teacher, and the story of Nachiketa is told to children and adults as a teaching on courage, truth and the self.

segments.voice: Yesterday, worn clothes, from the Bhagavad Gita. Your line was worn clothes. Did a garment remind you of the verse? Today, a new week, and a boy who goes to Death's own house. Day seven hundred seventy-one.

To whom will you give me? A boy asks his father that in the middle of a great sacrifice, where the father is giving away what he owns, including cows too old to give milk. The boy asks a second time. Then a third. And the father, losing patience, snaps: to Death I give you. That's how the Katha Upanishad, a Hindu scripture, begins. And the boy, Nachiketa, goes. Today: what he asks when he gets there.
screen: `TO WHOM WILL YOU GIVE ME?` → `TO DEATH I GIVE YOU.` → `AND THE BOY GOES.`

segments.voice: First, the waiting. Nachiketa reaches the house of Yama, lord of death, and Yama is away. The boy waits three nights without food. When Yama comes home he is troubled, because a guest has gone unfed in his house, and he offers three wishes, one for each night. Second, the question. Nachiketa spends his first wish on his father, that he'll be calm and glad to see him again. The second is to learn a sacred fire. The third is the question itself: when someone dies, some say they still are, and some say they are not. Teach me which. Third, the refusal. Yama tries to wriggle out of it. Even the gods have doubted about this, he says; it's subtle; ask for something else. And he lays out the alternatives: sons and grandsons, cattle and gold, horses, land, a long life, chariots and music. Nachiketa turns them all down. These things wear out, he says. Keep your horses, keep your songs. I want the answer. Fourth, the good and the pleasant. Only now does Yama begin to teach. Two things come to a person, he says: the good and the pleasant. The wise choose the good. What follows is his teaching on the self that is not born and does not die. Hindus read this Upanishad as scripture, and teachers keep coming back to Nachiketa. A boy at Death's door would rather have a true answer than everything Death can give him.
screen: `THREE NIGHTS AT DEATH'S HOUSE.` · `DO THEY STILL EXIST, OR NOT?` · `CHARIOTS AND GOLD, REFUSED.` · `THE GOOD OVER THE PLEASANT.` · then, large: `NACHIKETA'S QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Sit still and let your biggest question come up. Not the one you'd put on a form. The one underneath. It might be about death, or about a person, or about what any of this is for. When it arrives, say it to yourself in one plain sentence. You aren't trying to answer it. Just hold it, the way Nachiketa held his through three hungry nights. If other thoughts crowd in, come back to the sentence. The bell holds the time.
Nachiketa at Death's door: the boy in the Katha Upanishad who waits at Yama's house and asks what happens after death. Today's word.
Your line: Nachiketa's question. Today, write your biggest question down in one sentence, and keep it where you'll see it tonight. Day seven hundred seventy-one.

772.title: The ghats
772.hook: Hindus hold that dying in Kashi, Varanasi, brings liberation, and the cremation fires there never go out
772.howItsDone: Hindu families cremate their dead, and some bring them to the burning ghats at Varanasi, where a relative lights the pyre and the ashes are given to the Ganges; some people come to the city in old age hoping to die there.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nachiketa at Death's door. Your line was Nachiketa's question. Did you write yours down? Today, from a story to a real place: a city on a river. Day seven hundred seventy-two.

Stone steps run down into a wide river. At one end, people are bathing and praying in the water. A little further along, smoke rises from fires burning right on the steps. This is Varanasi, the city Hindus also call Kashi, on the Ganges. The steps are called ghats, and at some of them the dead are cremated in the open air. Tradition says those fires never go out. Today: why people come to this city at the end of their lives.
screen: `STEPS DOWN TO A RIVER.` → `SMOKE ON THE STEPS.` → `WHY COME HERE AT THE END?`

segments.voice: First, the steps. A ghat is a flight of steps leading down to the water. Along the river at Varanasi, ghat follows ghat. People come to bathe, to pray, to float small lamps at dusk. And a few of the ghats are for the dead. One is called Manikarnika. Second, the hope. Hindu tradition holds that to die in Kashi brings moksha, liberation from the cycle of birth and death. Texts that praise the city tell why: tradition says Shiva himself comes to the dying here and speaks a saving word into their ear, carrying them across. So some people come to Varanasi when they are old or ill, hoping to spend their last days in the city. Third, the fire. Cremation is the usual Hindu custom, though not the only one. At the burning ghats, the body, wrapped in cloth, is carried down through the lanes, dipped in the river, and laid on a pyre. A close relative lights it. Afterward the ashes are given to the Ganges. Tradition says the fires at Manikarnika have never been allowed to go out. Fourth, what this place does. Death is often kept behind a closed door. Here it happens on the steps, by the water, beside bathers, boats and children. The tradition doesn't treat this place as one of despair. It treats it as a place of release, kept in plain sight, in the middle of ordinary life.
screen: `STEPS DOWN TO THE WATER.` · `DIE IN KASHI, BE SET FREE.` · `THE FIRES ON THE STEPS.` · `DEATH IN PLAIN SIGHT.` · then, large: `THE GHATS.`

segments.voice: Light a small flame, if you have a candle and a safe place for it. If you don't, find any small light nearby and let that be your flame. At dusk on the river at Varanasi, people set little lamps on the water. Watch your flame. Notice how it moves and stays at once. If someone you've lost comes to mind, let them be there with the light. When the bell sounds, put the candle out, or leave it burning while you're in the room. The bell holds the time.
The ghats: the stone steps down to the river at Varanasi, where Hindus bathe, pray, and cremate their dead, hoping for liberation. Today's word.
Your line: the ghats. Today, when you see steps, or water, or a small flame, let it bring back the city that keeps death in plain sight. Day seven hundred seventy-two.

773.title: Praise, not death
773.hook: the mourner's prayer praises God and never mentions death
773.howItsDone: Jewish mourners say the Mourner's Kaddish at services with a minyan, during the period of mourning and on the anniversary of a death, and the congregation answers with amen and the response 'may his great name be blessed'.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ghats at Varanasi, where death is kept in plain sight. Your line was the ghats. Did a flame or a flight of steps bring them back? Today, Jewish voices, and a mourner's prayer. Day seven hundred seventy-three.

A mourner stands up in a synagogue, weeks after a funeral, and begins to speak in Aramaic. Around the room, people answer: amen. The prayer is the Kaddish, said by Jewish mourners for the people they have lost. Read it through, start to finish, and something is missing. It never mentions death. Not the person who died, not grief, not what comes after. Today: why the mourner's prayer is all praise.
screen: `A MOURNER STANDS.` → `THE ROOM ANSWERS: AMEN.` → `NO WORD ABOUT DEATH.`

segments.voice: First, the words. The Kaddish opens, yitgadal v'yitkadash sh'mei rabba: may God's great name be made great and holy. Then it keeps going: blessed, praised, glorified, lifted up. It even says God is beyond all the blessings and songs anyone can say. Second, the answer. The mourner doesn't carry it alone. The Kaddish is said with a minyan, a gathered quorum, and at its heart the whole room answers together: may his great name be blessed, forever and ever. Third, the ending. The last line asks for peace, for the people praying and for all Israel. It echoes a verse in the book of Job: "he maketh peace in his high places." Praise, then peace. And still no death. Fourth, why. Jewish teachers give more than one answer, and they don't cancel each other out. Some say the mourner, whose world has just gotten smaller, stands up in public and declares that God is still great: faith said aloud at the hardest moment. Tradition also holds that a child's Kaddish honors a parent who has died, so the praise is said for them, on their behalf. And some point to the room: the community's answer pulls the mourner back into the circle, again and again. A person in grief may have no words of their own. The Kaddish hands them old words, about something larger than the loss, and a room full of people to say amen.
screen: `MAY HIS GREAT NAME BE GREAT.` · `THE ROOM ANSWERS TOGETHER.` · `IT ENDS IN PEACE.` · `WHY PRAISE, AND NOT DEATH?` · then, large: `PRAISE, NOT DEATH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a life. Someone who has died, if there's someone you'd like to remember, or someone living, if that feels better today. Breathe, and let them be there. Then find one sentence of praise for that life: what was good in them, what they gave, what they made easier. Not a eulogy. One sentence. Say it silently, or quietly aloud. Then let the quiet hold it, the way a room holds the Kaddish. The bell holds the time.
Kaddish: the Jewish prayer said by mourners, mostly in Aramaic, that praises God, asks for peace, and never mentions death. Today's word.
Your line: praise, not death. Today, say your one sentence of praise for that life to someone else, aloud. Day seven hundred seventy-three.

774.title: We come to you
774.hook: mourners sit seven days and the community comes to them
774.howItsDone: After a funeral, Jewish mourners sit shiva at home, on low seats, while friends and neighbors visit, bring meals, join prayer services in the house, and offer a traditional word of comfort as they leave.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Kaddish. Your line was praise, not death. Did you say your sentence of praise aloud to someone? Today, what happens at home after the funeral. Day seven hundred seventy-four.

The front door is unlatched. Inside, the mirrors are covered and the family sits on low chairs. People come in without ringing, set food down on the kitchen counter, and sit, sometimes without saying anything at all. This is shiva, the week Jewish mourners keep at home after a funeral. The mourners don't go out to the world. The world comes to them. Today: the seven days, and the people who come.
screen: `AN UNLATCHED DOOR.` → `LOW CHAIRS, COVERED MIRRORS.` → `THE WORLD COMES TO THEM.`

segments.voice: First, the seven days. The custom reaches back into scripture. When Joseph buried his father Jacob, Genesis says simply, "he made a mourning for his father seven days." Second, the friends. When Job lost his children, his health and nearly everything else, his friends came and sat with him on the ground for seven days and nights, and the book says "none spake a word unto him." Before they ever argued with him, they sat. Third, the house. During shiva, mourners sit low, close to the ground. In some homes the mirrors are covered. The mourners don't cook or host; visitors bring the meals. Prayer services are often held right in the living room, so the mourner can say the Kaddish without leaving home. Fourth, the visitor. Tradition teaches that visitors should let the mourner speak first. If the mourner wants to talk about the person who died, you listen. If not, you sit. On the way out, visitors often say a traditional line asking that God comfort the mourner among the mourners of Zion and Jerusalem. That's the whole shape of it. Grief can shut a person in. Shiva reverses the direction. The one in pain doesn't have to find the strength to go anywhere or say anything. The community walks in the door, carrying soup, and says, without words: we come to you.
screen: `SEVEN DAYS FOR JACOB.` · `JOB'S FRIENDS SAT IN SILENCE.` · `LOW CHAIRS, NO COOKING.` · `LET THE MOURNER SPEAK FIRST.` · then, large: `WE COME TO YOU.`

segments.voice: Someone you know is carrying a loss. A loss this week, or one from years ago that still aches. Breathe, and let that person be there. Now plan, gently, how you could come to them: a visit, a call, a message that says you're thinking of them. You don't need the right words. A shiva visitor may say almost nothing. Decide only when, today or tomorrow. And if you're the one grieving, think instead of one person you'd let come. The bell holds the time.
Shiva: the week of mourning Jewish families keep at home after a funeral, when the community comes to them. Today's word.
Your line: we come to you. Today, visit or call the person you thought of, and let them speak first. Day seven hundred seventy-four.

775.title: Number our days
775.hook: teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom
775.howItsDone: In some Jewish communities Psalm 90 is prayed in the morning prayers of the Sabbath and festivals, and it is sometimes read at funerals; Christians read it too, in their own services.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shiva, the week when the community comes to the mourner. Your line was we come to you. Did you call or visit? Today, a psalm that asks to learn how to count. Day seven hundred seventy-five.

"So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom." That's one verse from Psalm 90, the psalm whose heading calls it a prayer of Moses, the man of God. It sounds almost like a math lesson. Count your days. But the psalm around it is about how short a human life is, and it doesn't ask for more days. It asks to count the ones there are. Today: what counting has to do with wisdom.
screen: `TEACH US TO NUMBER OUR DAYS.` → `A PRAYER OF MOSES.` → `WHY COUNT?`

segments.voice: First, God's clock. The psalm opens wide, with God before the mountains were born, and then says: "For a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past, and as a watch in the night." Time that feels endless to us passes, for God, like one short watch. Second, the grass. People, the psalm says, are like grass: "In the morning it flourisheth, and groweth up; in the evening it is cut down, and withereth." One day, start to finish. Third, the count. The psalm puts numbers on it: seventy years, eighty if there's strength, "for it is soon cut off, and we fly away." And then, right after, comes the verse: teach us to number our days. Not to dread them, and not to bargain for more. To count them, so that we bring home a heart of wisdom. Counting is how you notice that something is limited, and noticing is how you start to treat it with care. Fourth, where it lands. The psalm doesn't end on the grass. Its last words ask for something to last: "establish thou the work of our hands." Count the days, and then let the work done in them matter. In some Jewish communities this psalm is part of the Sabbath and festival morning prayers, and it is sometimes read at funerals. In a service of praise or beside a grave, the same verse sits in the middle of it, asking for a lesson in counting.
screen: `A THOUSAND YEARS AS YESTERDAY.` · `GRASS BY EVENING.` · `SOON CUT OFF, AND WE FLY AWAY.` · `ESTABLISH THE WORK OF OUR HANDS.` · then, large: `NUMBER OUR DAYS.`

segments.voice: Count today. Not the ones left. Just this one. On each breath out, count one thing this day has already held: waking up, a cup of something warm, a voice, a stretch of quiet, a task done. If you run out, count the things still ahead before you sleep. If you pray, you can say the psalm's line, so teach us to number our days. Otherwise, just keep counting, slowly, and notice that the day is full of things. The bell holds the time.
Number our days: Psalm 90's request to learn to count our days, so that we gain a heart of wisdom. Today's word.
Your line: number our days. Tonight, before you sleep, name one thing from today that you want to have counted. Day seven hundred seventy-five.

776.title: A time to die
776.hook: to every thing a season: a time to be born, and a time to die
776.howItsDone: Jews read Ecclesiastes as part of the Hebrew Bible, and some communities read the whole book at Sukkot; Christians read it too, and its list of times is sometimes read at funerals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Psalm 90. Your line was number our days. What did you count before you slept? Today, another book of the Hebrew Bible, and a list of times. Day seven hundred seventy-six.

What season is it? Not on the calendar. In a life. The book of Ecclesiastes has an answer, and it comes as a list. "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven: A time to be born, and a time to die." And the list goes on from there, pair after pair. Today: why dying sits right near the top of it.
screen: `WHAT SEASON IS IT?` → `A TIME TO BE BORN.` → `AND A TIME TO DIE.`

segments.voice: First, the speaker. Ecclesiastes is spoken by someone the Hebrew calls Koheleth, rendered in English as the Teacher or the Preacher. He has looked hard at everything done under the sun, and all of it, he says, is vanity, a word some readers hear as breath or vapor: real, and gone quickly. Second, the list. Then he lays out the times of a life in pairs. Born and die. Plant and pluck up. Break down and build up. "A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance." A time to keep silence, and a time to speak. Third, the pairing. Death isn't hidden at the end of the list or left off it. It's the second thing named, right beside being born. The list doesn't say which times are good and which are bad. It says each one has its time, and a life holds them all. Fourth, beauty in its time. A few verses later the Teacher writes, "He hath made every thing beautiful in his time: also he hath set the world in their heart." Some readers translate that word not as world but as eternity. Either way, it names something odd about being human: we live inside one season, and still long to see the whole. The Teacher doesn't fix that. He leaves the list standing. Some Jewish communities read the whole of Ecclesiastes at Sukkot, the harvest festival, a joyful time, listening to a book that never looks away from death.
screen: `THE TEACHER: VANITY, VAPOR.` · `A LIST OF TIMES, IN PAIRS.` · `DEATH BESIDE BIRTH.` · `BEAUTIFUL IN ITS TIME.` · then, large: `A TIME FOR EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: Run the Teacher's list through your own life. Planting or uprooting. Breaking down or building up. Weeping or laughing. Mourning or dancing. Keeping silence or speaking. Let each pair pass by slowly with your breath. When one of them catches, stay there. Maybe it's two at once; the list allows that. Just name the season you're in, in a word or two, without judging whether it's a good one. The bell holds the time.
A time to die: from the Teacher's list in Ecclesiastes, where death is named beside birth, each in its season. Today's word.
Your line: a time for everything. Today, tell one person the season you named, and ask them which season they're in. Day seven hundred seventy-six.

screen: `DAY 776 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE RESURRECTION AND THE LIFE.`

777.title: The resurrection and the life
777.hook: Jesus tells Martha: I am the resurrection and the life (John 11:25)
777.howItsDone: Some churches read John 11 at funerals, and in some burial services the words "I am the resurrection, and the life" are spoken at the graveside.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a time to be born and a time to die. Your line was a time for everything. What season did you name? Today closes the week, with Christian voices, and a sister standing on a road. Day seven hundred seventy-seven.

A house in Bethany, near Jerusalem. A man named Lazarus has died. His sisters, Martha and Mary, had sent word to their friend Jesus while Lazarus was still sick. He came late. When he arrives, John's Gospel says, Lazarus has already lain in the grave four days. Martha hears that Jesus is on the road and goes out to meet him. Mary stays in the house. Martha's first words are the ones a grieving person says at a hospital door: "Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died."
screen: `LAZARUS HAS DIED.` → `JESUS COMES LATE.` → `MARTHA GOES OUT TO MEET HIM.`

segments.voice: First, Martha already hopes. When Jesus tells her that her brother will rise again, she answers with what she knows: "I know that he shall rise again in the resurrection at the last day." Her hope is real, but it's far away, at the end of everything. It doesn't help much on day fifteen. Second, I am. Jesus answers: "I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live." In John's telling, the hope Martha placed at the end of time is suddenly standing in front of her on a dusty road, with a name and a face. Third, a question, and tears. Jesus asks her plainly: "Believest thou this?" Martha says yes, and names him the Christ. Then, on the way to the tomb, before anything is mended, two words: "Jesus wept." Only after the weeping does he call, "Lazarus, come forth," and the dead man walks out still wrapped in grave clothes. Christians read this as a sign, a return to this life. The hope they hold is larger: that because Jesus himself rose from the dead, the dead will be raised. Churches describe the details in their own ways, and in some churches this line is read at funerals and spoken at gravesides. Fourth, the week. Nachiketa's question at Death's door. The fires on the ghats. A mourner's prayer of praise. Neighbors who come to the house. Numbered days. A time for everything. And today, one tradition's hope said out loud. Whether or not it's your hope, it can be heard as Christians say it: christians hope this.
